source.title: The Norm-Separation Delay Law of Grokking: A First-Principles Theory of Delayed Generalization
source.authors: Xuan Khanh Truong; Truong Quynh Hoa; Trung Duc Luu; D. Phan

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some equations and figure text are affected by web-text formatting, but the relevant experimental tables and descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It tests delayed generalization and its proposed norm-separation mechanism using training runs, norm and spectral measurements, and hyperparameter sweeps; these are conceptual tests rather than a direct replication of the original studies.
record.gate_note: The study uses a fixed 50% training fraction and does not sweep training-set size, so it does not test whether smaller training sets require more optimization. Its results about initialization scale, non-algorithmic data, and realistic LLM training are not tests of the corresponding claim versions. Statements about prior work are not recorded as results. It reports its own norm-based delay predictor, which is included because it measures whether a progress measure predicts the generalization delay.
record.test_reason: The study trains one-layer transformers on modular addition and multiplication, and MLPs on sparse parity. It measures memorisation time, grokking time and the delay between them, and tracks parameter norm and non-Fourier energy. It sweeps weight decay, learning rate, modulus and optimizer. These results bear on V1 (delayed generalisation on algorithmic data), V2 (whether a continuous measure anticipates the jump) and V5 (weight decay / low-norm bias favouring the generalising solution). The method differs from the originals: it fixes the training fraction at 50% and does no circuit analysis. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that grokking delay is Θ((1/γeff)·log(Vmem/Vpost)) under regularised first-order training. They give matching upper and lower bounds and prove norm separation is necessary. They report that it is confirmed on modular addition and multiplication and correctly predicts no grokking on sparse parity. They report that grokking needs an optimizer that can memorise first (AdamW yes, SGD at λ = 1 no). They also offer a delay predictor with 34.6% mean absolute error.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular arithmetic grokking with a one-layer transformer and accuracy thresholds, but focuses on norm contraction, Fourier energy, and delay-law validation rather than reproducing the original training-set-size experiments or mechanistic-circuit analysis. Training fraction is fixed at 50%; optimizer and weight-decay/learning-rate sweeps are added.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes depend on weight decay: no grokking for λ ≤ 0.01, reliable grokking for λ ∈ [0.1, 1.0], and rare or absent grokking at λ ≥ 2.0. At λ = 1.0, AdamW groks but SGD fails to memorise under both tested decay conventions. Sparse parity has no delayed transition and an inverted norm ratio. Learning-rate sweep increases reported Tgrok as η decreases.

fits_no_version.finding: The grokking delay scales quantitatively with log(Vmem/Vpost)/(ηλ). The delay correlates with the predicted escape time (Pearson r = 0.91, 49 runs), Tgrok fits 1/λ (R2 = 0.971) and 1/η (R2 = 0.92), and an at-memorisation predictor gives 34.6% mean error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The length of the grokking delay is set by the log ratio of memorisation to generalising norm divided by the effective weight-decay contraction rate.

record.problems: No training-set-size sweep, despite the claim's training-set-size prediction. Experimental model/task coverage is limited to modular addition, modular multiplication, and sparse parity; no natural-data or LLM experiment is run. The spectral analysis uses 5 seeds and samples energy every 500 steps. The validation-gap OLS fit is weaker than the reported inlier fit, with R2 = 0.769 and 50% of points classified as RANSAC outliers. The delay predictor is evaluated on 60 seeds from the same modular-addition setup. The SGD comparison fails to memorise, so it does not compare post-overfitting delays across optimizers.

untested.parts: Dependence of delay on training-set size: the training fraction is fixed at 50%, with no fraction sweep.

Identification of a generalising circuit forming gradually, and later removal of memorising components (a cleanup phase). Only the aggregate non-Fourier energy fraction is measured, at 500-step resolution.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic data and no initialisation-scale or lazy-to-rich manipulation. Weight decay switches grokking on and off, but only on algorithmic tasks.
Not tested: no LLM or realistic data.
Critical dataset size and ungrokking below it: there is no dataset-size sweep.
Not tested: no comparison of algorithms across runs.
Not tested: SGD vs AdamW is not a control for adaptive-optimizer instabilities or numerical precision.

missing.what: Joint η×λ grid (η in {2e-3, 1e-3, 5e-4}, λ in {0.5, 1, 2}, 5 seeds per cell): mean Tgrok·ηλ = 9.58, CV about 2.7.
Delay vs theoretical escape time across the 49 modulus runs: Pearson r = 0.91, slope 1.08 ± 0.15. Cross-task addition+multiplication: r = 0.90.
High-resolution spectral re-run: K* = 23, OLS R2 = 0.767, RANSAC R2 = 0.852.

record.verdict_notes: The training fraction is fixed at 50%. In the modulus sweep the absolute training-set size grows with p (p²/2 pairs), and delay falls from 2086 to 585 steps. This is loosely consistent with V1's size dependence but confounded by task size, so it is not used as a verdict. Weak-λ runs were capped at 15k steps, so 'no grokking' may mean not yet. Sparse parity uses a different architecture (MLP) and unstated data size. The paper is mainly theoretical; its interpretive claims (e.g. the RANSAC outlier explanation) are the authors' own.

versions.untested_parts: The effect of training-set size on delay is not tested: the modular-addition setup uses 50% training data, with no training-fraction sweep.

The study measures non-Fourier energy and norm contraction, but does not identify and track memorizing circuit components being removed, or directly test a Fourier-circuit progress measure that anticipates the accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule task; no initialization-scale sweep or explicit lazy-to-rich transition test.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
The study tests weight-decay and norm-separation predictions, but does not sweep dataset size to establish a critical dataset size or test ungrokking below that size.
It does not compare identifiable algorithms across runs or test whether networks converge to the same algorithm.
The SGD-versus-AdamW comparison is not a control for adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax limits; no numerical-precision intervention is reported.
